mainTopic: Cleanliness for קריאת שמע and תפלה: covering the body, תפילין in a בית הכסא, bad smells, and nearby צואה and מי רגלים
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier ruling: for תפלה one must cover his heart. רב הונא then teaches that someone who entered a בית הכסא wearing תפילין covers them with his hand until the first discharge is done, because holding back is a health danger. רב הונא and רב חסדא disagree about saying קריאת שמע when there is צואה on the skin or a hand is inside a בית הכסא. They also disagree about how far to move from a bad smell, and רבא limits which kinds of animal filth matter. רב ששת rules on a smell with no source, and אביי and רבא argue about צואה that is passing by. The גמרא then treats doubtful צואה and מי רגלים and explains why the חכמים did not forbid doubtful מי רגלים. It also asks how long dried צואה and מי רגלים still forbid holy speech. רבא rules that צואה dry like earthenware is still forbidden and מי רגלים are forbidden while they moisten. The amud ends by testing whether a dispute between תנאים matches this question; the גמרא's answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: For prayer, one must cover his heart
steps.stepSummary: This line finishes a ruling from the previous page. A lower body covering may be enough for קריאת שמע, but תפלה requires the heart to be covered too.
steps.simpleTranslation: But for prayer, he may not pray until he covers his heart.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a rule that began on the previous page. For תפלה there is a stricter dress requirement: the heart area must be covered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous page dealt with a minimal covering that is enough for קריאת שמע. Here the גמרא adds that תפלה is different. In תפלה a person stands and speaks directly to הקב"ה, so he must be dressed more fully, at least up to the heart.
steps.confusionAlert: This line is the END of an earlier discussion, not a new topic. The word אבל ('but') contrasts תפלה with קריאת שמע from the lines just before.

phrases.english: But for prayer
phrases.notes: Contrasts with the more lenient rule for קריאת שמע on the previous page

phrases.english: [he may not pray] until he covers his heart.
phrases.notes: Prayer is speaking directly before God, so one must be properly dressed

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל לִתְפִלָּה עַד שֶׁיְּכַסֶּה אֶת לִבּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a ruling begun on the previous page
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תפלה requires covering the heart, which is stricter than the requirement for קריאת שמע.

steps.title: Entering the בית הכסא while wearing תפילין by mistake
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules: if someone forgot and entered a בית הכסא wearing תפילין, he puts his hand on them until he finishes.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב הונא said: If someone forgot and went into the בית הכסא wearing תפילין, he places his hand over them until he finishes.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ruling from רב הונא. It covers someone who walked into the בית הכסא and only then realized he was still wearing תפילין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally you may not bring תפילין into a בית הכסא. Since this person entered by accident, רב הונא gives a practical fix: cover the תפילין with your hand. The phrase 'until he finishes' sounds odd, and the גמרא will question it next.

keyTerms.meaning: The תפילין worn on the head and arm
He places his hand on them (covering them)

phrases.english: And Rav Huna said:
[If] he forgot and entered while wearing tefillin
into the bathroom —
he places his hand on them
until he finishes.
phrases.notes: This phrase is about to be challenged

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב הוּנָא: שָׁכַח וְנִכְנַס בִּתְפִילִּין לְבֵית הַכִּסֵּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New ruling on a related topic: respect for holy objects in an unclean place
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who accidentally entered a בית הכסא with תפילין covers them with his hand until he finishes.

steps.title: Can he really stay until he is completely done?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to the wording 'until he finishes.' Can it really mean he stays there with תפילין until he is fully done?
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Until he finishes' — could you really think so?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב הונא's words. It cannot be that he may stay the whole time wearing תפילין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'until he finishes' meant until he is completely done, it would allow a long stay in the בית הכסא with holy תפילין on. That would be a serious disrespect. So the wording must mean something more limited.

keyTerms.meaning: Would it enter your mind? (expresses disbelief)

phrases.english: 'Until he finishes' — could that enter your mind?!
phrases.notes: Rhetorical disbelief: the plain reading is impossible

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording of רב הונא's ruling
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase עד שיגמור in רב הונא's ruling
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Read literally, it allows staying the whole time in a בית הכסא wearing תפילין, which cannot be.

steps.title: It means until the first discharge is finished
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק explains: 'until he finishes' means only until the first עמוד (first mass of waste) is done. Then he leaves and removes the תפילין.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, as רב נחמן בר יצחק said: until he finishes the first mass.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It narrows 'until he finishes' to a short window: just the first discharge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling is not thrown out. It is reinterpreted. He stays only for the first unavoidable discharge, then steps out and takes off the תפילין. This keeps the time with תפילין in the בית הכסא as short as possible.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא כִּדְאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: Rather, as Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:
until he finishes the first mass.
phrases.notes: After that he goes out and removes the תפילין

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כִּדְאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא by reinterpreting the wording
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Until he finishes' means until he is completely done.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means only until the first עמוד is finished.

steps.title: Why not stop immediately and get up?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: why wait even for the first discharge? Let him stop right away and get up.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him stop immediately and get up!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes further. Even waiting for the first discharge seems too long, so why not leave at once?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן בר יצחק shortened the time, but there is still some time with תפילין in the בית הכסא. Out of respect for the תפילין, the ideal would seem to be stopping right away. The גמרא wants to know why that is not required.

keyTerms.meaning: And let him stop / cut off

phrases.english: But let him stop immediately and get up?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of רב נחמן בר יצחק
steps.kashyaTarget: The allowance to wait until the first עמוד is finished
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Respect for תפילין should require stopping and leaving immediately.

steps.title: Holding back is a health danger
steps.stepSummary: He may not stop in the middle because of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's teaching. Holding back waste causes serious illness.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, as it was taught: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: A mass of feces held back brings a person to dropsy; a stream of urine held back brings a person to jaundice.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that stopping in the middle is a health risk. It proves this from a ברייתא of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding back stool can cause הדרוקן (dropsy, swelling with fluid). Holding back urine can cause ירקון (jaundice). Because of this danger, חז"ל did not require him to stop. He finishes the first discharge while covering the תפילין, then leaves.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
A mass of feces that is held back
A stream of urine that is held back

steps.whatToRemember: With תפילין in a בית הכסא by mistake: cover them with your hand, finish only the first discharge, then go out and remove them. You do not stop in the middle, because holding back is dangerous to health.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that חז"ל weighed respect for holy objects against real danger to health, and health won out for this short time.

phrases.english: Because of [the teaching of] Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel,

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר,
phrases.english: as it was taught: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says,
a mass [of feces] that is held back —
brings a person to dropsy,
a stream [of urine] that is held back —
brings a person to jaundice.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל, דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers why he cannot stop immediately
steps.terutzResolutionType: Overriding concern (health danger) backed by a ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He should stop at once out of respect for the תפילין.
steps.terutzMaskana: Stopping in the middle is dangerous, so he finishes the first discharge while covering the תפילין.

steps.title: Dispute: קריאת שמע with filth on the body or a hand in the בית הכסא
steps.stepSummary: A new מחלוקת: may a person say קריאת שמע if there is צואה on his skin, or if his hand is inside a בית הכסא? רב הונא permits it; רב חסדא forbids it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: If there is צואה on his skin, or his hand is placed inside the בית הכסא — רב הונא said: he may recite קריאת שמע. רב חסדא said: he may not recite קריאת שמע.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new dispute between אמוראים. The question is whether one unclean body part blocks a person from saying קריאת שמע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases most of the person, including his mouth, is in a clean place, and only one part of his body is unclean. רב הונא is lenient and רב חסדא is strict. The next steps will give each one's reason.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (introduces an אמוראים dispute)

phrases.english: It was stated: [If there is] feces on his skin,
or his hand is placed inside the bathroom,
phrases.notes: Only the hand is there; the rest of him is outside

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא אָמַר: מוּתָּר לִקְרוֹת קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע.
phrases.english: Rav Huna said: he is permitted to recite Shema.
Rav Ḥisda said:
he is forbidden to recite Shema.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִתְּמַר: צוֹאָה עַל בְּשָׂרוֹ, אוֹ יָדוֹ מוּנַּחַת בְּבֵית הַכִּסֵּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New מחלוקת on a related theme: cleanliness while saying holy words
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב הונא permits קריאת שמע when only part of the body is unclean; רב חסדא forbids it.

steps.title: רב הונא's source: let every breath praise God
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains רב הונא's reason from the פסוק 'כל הנשמה תהלל יה.' What praises God is the breath, so only the mouth must be in a clean place.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: What is רב הונא's reason? As it is written: 'Let every soul praise the Lord, Halleluyah.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the source for רב הונא's lenient view. It is a פסוק from תהלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא reads נשמה as connected to נשימה (breath). The praise comes from the breath and mouth. So as long as the mouth is in a clean place, a dirty hand or skin does not matter.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָבָא: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַב הוּנָא —
phrases.english: Rava said: What is the reason of Rav Huna?
As it is written: 'Let every soul praise the Lord, Halleluyah' (Psalms 150:6).
phrases.notes: Read as 'every breath': the praise comes from the mouth

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning behind רב הונא's side of the dispute
steps.raayaObject: רב הונא's ruling that one may say קריאת שמע when only part of the body is unclean
steps.raayaSupportSource: תהלים קנ:ו — כל הנשמה תהלל יה

steps.title: רב חסדא's source: all my bones shall praise
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא repeats רב חסדא's strict view in order to give his reason. The פסוק 'כל עצמותי תאמרנה' shows that the whole body takes part in praising God.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב חסדא said: he may not recite קריאת שמע. What is רב חסדא's reason? As it is written: 'All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like You.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא restates רב חסדא's ruling so it can give his source. That source is also a פסוק from תהלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא says that praise of God involves the entire body, every bone. So if even one part, like a hand or a patch of skin, is in an unclean state, he may not say קריאת שמע. This is the direct opposite of רב הונא's focus on the mouth alone.
steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא: only the mouth needs to be clean (כל הנשמה, the breath praises). רב חסדא: the whole body must be clean (כל עצמותי, all the bones praise).
steps.confusionAlert: Repeating רב חסדא's ruling is not a new opinion or a new step in the argument. The גמרא restates it only to attach his reason to it.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר: אָסוּר לִקְרוֹת קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע.
phrases.english: And Rav Ḥisda said: he is forbidden to recite Shema.
What is the reason of Rav Ḥisda?

phrases.aramaic: דִּכְתִיב: ״כׇּל עַצְמוֹתַי תֹּאמַרְנָה ה׳ מִי כָמוֹךָ״.
phrases.english: As it is written: 'All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like You' (Psalms 35:10).
phrases.notes: The whole body takes part in the praise

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר: אָסוּר לִקְרוֹת קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע. מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing reasoning, matching רב הונא's source in step 8
steps.raayaObject: רב חסדא's ruling that one may not say קריאת שמע if any part of the body is unclean
steps.raayaSupportSource: תהלים לה:י — כל עצמותי תאמרנה ה׳ מי כמוך

steps.title: How far to move from a bad smell that has a visible source
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא says to move four אמות from the source of the smell. רב חסדא says to move four אמות from the point where the smell stops.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was said: if there is a bad smell that comes from something you can see, רב הונא says a person moves four אמות away and then says קריאת שמע. רב חסדא says he moves four אמות past the place where the smell ends, and then says קריאת שמע.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new מחלוקת about a bad smell that comes from a real, visible source, like a pile of filth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both agree you must move four אמות away. They disagree about where you start counting. For רב הונא you count from the filth itself, while for רב חסדא you count from where the smell can no longer be noticed, which can be much farther away.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It was said': it introduces a מחלוקת between אמוראים
That has a source, meaning a visible thing that the smell comes from

phrases.aramaic: אִתְּמַר: רֵיחַ רַע שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ עִיקָּר —
phrases.english: It was said: a bad smell that has a source —

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא אָמַר: מַרְחִיק אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת,
phrases.english: Rav Huna said: he moves four cubits away,
phrases.notes: Counted from the source of the smell.

phrases.english: and recites Shema.
And Rav Chisda said:

phrases.aramaic: מַרְחִיק אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת מִמְּקוֹם שֶׁפָּסַק הָרֵיחַ,
phrases.english: he moves four cubits away from the place where the smell stopped,
and recites Shema.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִתְּמַר: רֵיחַ רַע שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ עִיקָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new מחלוקת between the same two אמוראים, רב הונא and רב חסדא, on a related topic: a smell instead of direct contact with צואה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב הונא: four אמות from the source. רב חסדא: four אמות from where the smell ends.

steps.title: A ברייתא that supports רב חסדא
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists kinds of filth you may not say קריאת שמע near, explains when a height difference helps, and ends by saying to move four אמות from the place of the smell, matching רב חסדא.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא was taught that agrees with רב חסדא: A person may not say קריאת שמע facing human צואה, dog צואה, pig צואה, chicken צואה, or a garbage heap that smells bad. If the filth is ten טפחים higher or lower than him, he may sit next to it and say קריאת שמע. If not, he must move away until it is out of his sight. The same goes for תפילה. For a bad smell that has a source, he moves four אמות from the place of the smell and then says קריאת שמע.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא to show that רב חסדא's view has support from a תנאי source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is in the last line. The ברייתא says to move four אמות 'from the place of the smell', which means from where the smell is still felt, not from the filth itself. That is exactly רב חסדא's view. The rest of the ברייתא adds useful details: a ten-טפחים height difference makes it a separate area, and filth you can see requires moving until it is out of sight.

keyTerms.meaning: 'A ברייתא was taught in agreement with him': it introduces support
Ten handbreadths. A height difference this size makes it a separate area
As far as his eyes can see, meaning until it is out of sight

steps.confusionAlert: 'מִמְּקוֹם הָרֵיחַ' does not mean 'from the filth.' It means from the area where the smell reaches, so you count from where the smell ends. That is why the line supports רב חסדא and not רב הונא.

phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita in agreement with Rav Chisda:
A person may not recite Shema,
not facing human excrement,
and not facing dog excrement,
and not facing pig excrement,
and not facing chicken excrement,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא כְּנֶגֶד צוֹאַת אַשְׁפָּה שֶׁרֵיחָהּ רָע.
phrases.english: and not facing the filth of a dung heap that smells bad.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם הָיָה מָקוֹם גָּבוֹהַּ עֲשָׂרָה טְפָחִים
phrases.english: But if it was in a place ten handbreadths higher
or ten handbreadths lower —
he may sit beside it and recite Shema.
phrases.notes: The height difference makes it a separate area.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם לָאו — מַרְחִיק מִמֶּנּוּ מְלוֹא עֵינָיו.
phrases.english: And if not, he moves away from it as far as his eyes can see.
And the same applies to prayer.
A bad smell that has a source —
he moves four cubits away from the place of the smell,
phrases.notes: This is the line that matches רב חסדא.

phrases.english: and recites Shema.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב חסדא's side of the מחלוקת in step 10.
steps.raayaObject: רב חסדא's rule that you count four אמות from where the smell ends.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that says 'מרחיק ארבע אמות ממקום הריח'.

steps.title: רבא rules that the הלכה follows a narrower ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the הלכה does not follow all the rulings of the first ברייתא. It follows another ברייתא, which forbids only human צואה, pig צואה, and dog צואה that had hides put into it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The הלכה does not follow this ברייתא in all of its rulings. It follows the other ברייתא, which teaches: A person may not say קריאת שמע facing human צואה, or facing pig צואה, or facing dog צואה when hides have been put into it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the practical הלכה. He does not accept the long list in the first ברייתא, and he follows a different ברייתא with a shorter list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא forbade many kinds of animal filth, including chicken droppings and any smelly dung heap. רבא narrows it down: only human צואה, pig צואה, and dog צואה used for tanning hides are a problem, because these smell especially bad. Other animal droppings do not stop a person from saying קריאת שמע.

keyTerms.meaning: The הלכה is not like this
A ברייתא, a teaching of the תנאים outside the משנה
Animal hides. Dog droppings were used in tanning them, which made a very strong smell

steps.whatToRemember: In practice, the list of forbidden filth is short: human צואה, pig צואה, and dog צואה used for tanning hides.

phrases.english: Rava said:
The halakha is not like this baraita
in all of these rulings,
rather, it is like that which was taught:
A person may not recite Shema
not facing human excrement,
and not facing pig excrement,
and not facing dog excrement
when one has put hides into it.
phrases.notes: Used in tanning, which made the smell very strong.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: לֵית הִלְכְתָא כִּי הָא מַתְנִיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the final הלכה about the ברייתא quoted in step 11 and narrows its list.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Only human צואה, pig צואה, and dog צואה used for tanning stop קריאת שמע. Other animal droppings do not.

steps.title: What about a bad smell with no visible source?
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת is asked about a bad smell that has no visible source.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked רב ששת: what is the law of a bad smell that has no source?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question is asked. The case is a smell that does not come from any visible filth, such as passed gas.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now, every case involved a smell coming from a real object. Here there is nothing to move away from, so the question is whether such a smell matters at all.

phrases.english: They asked Rav Sheshet:

phrases.aramaic: רֵיחַ רַע שֶׁאֵין לוֹ עִיקָּר, מַהוּ?
phrases.english: A bad smell that has no source, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from a smell with a source (step 10) to a smell without one.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a smell without a visible source stops a person from learning or saying קריאת שמע.

steps.title: רב ששת points to the mats in the בית המדרש
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers that in the בית המדרש some people sleep on the mats while others learn, and nobody worries about the smell.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Come and see these mats in the בית המדרש. Some people sleep on them and others learn, and they do not stop learning.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers by pointing to what people actually do in the בית המדרש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sleepers sometimes pass gas, yet the students next to them keep learning. This shows that a smell with no visible source does not stop learning.

keyTerms.meaning: The בית המדרש, the study hall

phrases.english: He said to them: Come and see
these mats of the study hall,
where these sleep and these learn.
phrases.notes: The learners are not bothered by any smell from the sleepers.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לְהוּ: אֲתוֹ חֲזוֹ הָנֵי צִיפֵּי דְבֵי רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A smell with no visible source does not stop learning, as we see from the בית המדרש.

steps.title: Two limits on רב ששת's answer
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת's leniency applies only to דברי תורה, not to קריאת שמע. Even for דברי תורה, it applies only to someone else's smell, not to one's own.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only to learning Torah, but not to קריאת שמע. And even for learning Torah, we only said it about someone else's smell, but not about his own.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows רב ששת's answer with two limits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First, the leniency is only for learning Torah. If people had to stop every time this happened, learning would always be interrupted, but קריאת שמע stays forbidden. Second, even in learning, it applies only when the smell came from another person. If the smell came from himself, he must stop.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And these words apply only to...': it introduces a limit

steps.whatToRemember: A smell with no source: it is allowed only for learning Torah, and only when it is someone else's smell. It is never allowed for קריאת שמע.

phrases.english: But this applies only to Torah study,
but not to the recitation of Shema.
And even for Torah study we only said it
about another person's smell,
but not about his own.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the leniency given in step 14.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A smell with no source is overlooked only for learning Torah and only when it is someone else's, never for קריאת שמע.

steps.title: A disagreement about passing filth
steps.stepSummary: אביי permits קריאת שמע near passing צואה; רבא forbids it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: Regarding passing feces, אביי says one may recite קריאת שמע, while רבא says one may not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא introduces a new disagreement: does the rule change when the צואה is moving rather than staying in one place?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both views address the same moving source. The question is whether its movement makes a difference for קריאת שמע.

phrases.english: It was stated: Passing feces—

phrases.aramaic: אַבָּיֵי אָמַר: מוּתָּר לִקְרוֹת קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע.
phrases.english: Abaye said: It is permitted to recite Shema.

phrases.aramaic: רָבָא אָמַר: אָסוּר לִקְרוֹת קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע.
phrases.english: Rava said: It is forbidden to recite Shema.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the limits of the earlier leniency about an unseen smell to a new case involving passing צואה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אביי permits קריאת שמע near passing צואה; רבא forbids it.

steps.title: אביי compares the case to טומאה under a tree
steps.stepSummary: אביי cites a משנה in which a passing source of טומאה has a different effect from one that stops.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: From where do I derive this? We learned: If an impure person stands under a tree and a pure person passes by, the pure person becomes impure. If the pure person stands under the tree and the impure person passes by, the pure person remains pure. If the impure person stops, the pure person becomes impure. The same applies to an afflicted stone.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי brings a משנה to support his view. He points to a case where stopping matters, but merely passing by does not have the same effect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the second arrangement, the passing impure person does not make the standing person impure; stopping changes the result. אביי uses that difference to suggest that passing צואה should not prevent קריאת שמע.

keyTerms.meaning: as we learned in a משנה

phrases.english: Abaye said: From where do I derive this?
As we learned: The impure person stands beneath the tree
and the pure person passes by—the pure person becomes impure.
The pure person stands beneath the tree
and the impure person passes by—the pure person remains pure.
But if the impure person stopped, the pure person becomes impure.
And the same applies to an afflicted stone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: מְנָא אָמֵינָא לַהּ — דִּתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: אביי supplies support for his permission in step 16.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that movement can change the rule for passing צואה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A משנה contrasting an impure person or afflicted stone that passes beneath a tree with one that stops there.

steps.title: רבא distinguishes the two laws
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that permanence matters in the cited טומאה case, while holiness of the camp governs the case of קריאת שמע.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא could tell you: There, the matter depends on being settled in a place, as it is written, “He shall dwell alone; outside the camp shall be his dwelling.” Here, the Torah said, “Your camp shall be holy,” and that condition is absent.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא rejects אביי’s comparison. He says the cited law asks whether the impure source has settled, while the present case asks whether the camp is holy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse about the impure person speaks of dwelling, so stopping is important in that case. רבא says passing צואה still conflicts with the separate requirement that one’s camp be holy.

phrases.aramaic: וְרָבָא אָמַר לָךְ: הָתָם בִּקְבִיעוּתָא תַּלְיָא מִילְּתָא,
phrases.english: And Rava could say to you: There, the matter depends on being settled in place,
as it is written: “He shall dwell alone;
outside the camp shall be his dwelling.”
Here, “And your camp shall be holy”
is what the Torah said, and that condition is not present.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרָבָא אָמַר לָךְ: הָתָם בִּקְבִיעוּתָא תַּלְיָא מִילְּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the comparison used as אביי’s proof.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: אביי’s use of the טומאה case as proof for the law of passing צואה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The טומאה case has a dwelling-based rule; the קריאת שמע case has a holiness-of-the-camp requirement.

steps.title: A pig’s mouth is compared to passing filth
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא applies the category of passing צואה to a pig’s mouth.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: A pig’s mouth is like passing feces.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא introduces a related case. He treats a pig’s mouth as comparable to צואה עוֹבֶרֶת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pig is moving, so its mouth supplies a concrete case for the earlier discussion of a moving source. The next line asks what this statement adds.

keyTerms.meaning: the אמורא who makes this comparison

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: A pig’s mouth
is like passing feces.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רבא’s response, the גמרא moves to a related example of something moving.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A pig’s mouth is treated like passing צואה.

steps.title: What does the pig’s-mouth ruling add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב פפא’s statement as obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב פפא needed to say this. At first, the comparison seems self-evident.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a pig’s mouth is plainly comparable to passing צואה, the statement appears to teach nothing new. The challenge prepares for a less obvious case.

phrases.english: That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for רב פפא’s statement.
steps.kashyaTarget: The apparent novelty of רב פפא’s comparison.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Without a special circumstance, the comparison seems too obvious to require a separate statement.

steps.title: The ruling includes a pig just out of the river
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא’s statement is needed even when the pig has come out of a river.
steps.simpleTranslation: No; the statement is needed even when the pig has come up from the river.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא identifies the surprising case: the pig has just left a river. רב פפא’s comparison still applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think the river cleaned the pig’s mouth. The answer says that this does not remove the concern addressed by רב פפא’s statement.

keyTerms.meaning: no; the statement is needed for a case where

steps.whatToRemember: רב פפא includes even a pig that has just left the river in his comparison to צואה עוֹבֶרֶת.

phrases.english: No; it is needed even though
it came up from the river.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא אַף עַל גַּב דְּסָלֵיק מִנַּהֲרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers why רב פפא’s apparently obvious statement was necessary.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies a less obvious case included in the ruling.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Coming out of the river might have cleaned the pig’s mouth enough to change its treatment.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב פפא’s comparison applies even after the pig comes out of the river.

steps.title: Two kinds of doubt receive different rulings
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה prohibits sacred speech when צואה may be present, but permits it when מי רגלים may be present.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: Doubtful צואה is prohibited; doubtful מי רגלים are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה states the basic difference between the two doubts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is about uncertainty over whether the substance is present. The ruling is stricter for צואה than for מי רגלים.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: סְפֵק צוֹאָה — אֲסוּרָה.
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: Doubtful feces is prohibited.
Doubtful urine is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the discussion of passing צואה, the גמרא turns to uncertainty about צואה and מי רגלים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Doubtful צואה is prohibited; doubtful מי רגלים are permitted.

steps.title: Another version takes the location into account
steps.stepSummary: A second version of רב יהודה permits doubtful צואה in a house but prohibits it at a dung heap. Doubtful מי רגלים remain permitted even at a dung heap.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say רב יהודה said: Doubtful צואה is permitted in a house and prohibited at a dung heap. Doubtful מי רגלים are permitted even at a dung heap.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another version of רב יהודה’s ruling. This version adds the location of the doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A house and a dung heap do not create the same level of concern about צואה. The added distinction does not change the lenient ruling for doubtful מי רגלים.

phrases.english: Some say: Rav Yehuda said:
Doubtful feces in a house is permitted,
but at a dung heap it is prohibited.

phrases.aramaic: סְפֵק מֵי רַגְלַיִם — אֲפִילּוּ בָּאַשְׁפָּה נָמֵי מוּתָּרִין.
phrases.english: Doubtful urine is permitted even at a dung heap.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is an alternative wording of רב יהודה’s ruling, not a challenge to it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this version, location matters for doubtful צואה, while doubtful מי רגלים are permitted even at a dung heap.

steps.title: The Torah-level limit concerns the stream itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא connects the lenient ruling about doubtful מי רגלים to רב המנונא’s statement that the תורה prohibits sacred speech only opposite the stream.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds like רב המנונא, who said: The תורה prohibited it only opposite the stream itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins explaining the leniency about doubtful מי רגלים by bringing רב המנונא’s rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב המנונא speaks about מי רגלים while they are flowing. The next steps will explain what that limit means once they have reached the ground.

keyTerms.meaning: the אמורא whose rule explains the leniency

phrases.aramaic: סָבַר לַהּ כִּי הָא דְּרַב הַמְנוּנָא,
phrases.english: He holds like this teaching of Rav Hamnuna,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב הַמְנוּנָא: לֹא אָסְרָה תּוֹרָה
phrases.english: for Rav Hamnuna said: The Torah prohibited it
only opposite the stream itself.

steps.triggerLanguage: סָבַר לַהּ כִּי הָא דְּרַב הַמְנוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא starts supplying a reason for the permissive ruling about doubtful מי רגלים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The תורה-level prohibition concerning מי רגלים applies opposite the flowing stream.

steps.title: Two verses describe different requirements
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן places a verse about going outside alongside a verse about covering excrement, setting up a question about their different requirements.
steps.simpleTranslation: And like רבי יונתן, who raised this difficulty: One verse says to have a place outside the camp and go there; another says to have a spade and cover your excrement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא prepares the next explanation by quoting רבי יונתן’s comparison of two verses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One verse mentions going outside. The other also requires covering what was passed. רבי יונתן asks how these different instructions fit together.

keyTerms.meaning: sets two sources against each other

phrases.english: And like Rabbi Yonatan; for Rabbi Yonatan set these verses against each other:
It is written: “You shall have a designated place
outside the camp, and you shall go out there,”
and it is written: “You shall have a spade,” and so forth,
“and you shall cover your excrement.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא brings רבי יונתן’s reading of the verses to explain רב המנונא’s limit.
steps.kashyaTarget: How to read the two verses’ different instructions together.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One verse requires going outside, while the other adds a requirement to cover excrement.

steps.title: The verses address different bodily needs
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן resolves the difference: one instruction concerns feces, and the other concerns urine.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can both verses be understood? One concerns a bowel movement, and one concerns urination.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves רבי יונתן’s question by separating the two cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The covering requirement applies to צואה. The instruction about going outside also addresses מי רגלים, without giving them that same covering requirement.

phrases.english: How is this understood? Here it concerns a bowel movement,
and here it concerns urination.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This answers the difference רבי יונתן identified between the verses.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The different instructions might seem to apply to the same bodily need.
steps.terutzMaskana: The covering instruction concerns צואה; the verses also address מי רגלים.

steps.title: The verse supports the distinction between a stream and urine on the ground
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws out רבי יונתן’s implication: the תורה-level prohibition for מי רגלים applies opposite the stream, not after they land.
steps.simpleTranslation: It follows that the תורה prohibited urination only opposite the stream. Once it has fallen to the ground, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws an inference from רבי יונתן’s answer and uses it to support רב המנונא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה-level rule concerns the act of urination while the stream is present. Urine already on the ground therefore has a different outcome under that rule.

phrases.english: It follows that the Torah prohibited urination
only opposite the stream itself.
But once it has fallen to the ground, it is permitted,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא states what רבי יונתן’s distinction shows about the תורה-level rule.
steps.raayaObject: רב המנונא’s rule that the תורה-level prohibition concerning מי רגלים applies opposite the stream.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יונתן’s distinction between the instructions in the two verses.

steps.title: The later restriction applies only when urine is certainly present
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים restricted sacred speech near urine on the ground, but their restriction applies to definite urine, not doubtful urine.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages decreed concerning it. But when they decreed, they did so for urine certainly present; they did not decree for doubtful urine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the explanation of why doubtful מי רגלים are permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Permission under the תורה-level rule does not mean there is never a restriction near urine on the ground: the חכמים added one. They applied it when urine is certainly present, which leaves the doubtful case permitted.
steps.whatToRemember: For מי רגלים, separate the two levels: the תורה-level prohibition concerns the flowing stream; the חכמים’s restriction on urine after it lands applies when it is certainly present, not when its presence is doubtful.

phrases.english: And it was the Sages who decreed concerning it,
and when the Sages decreed, it was when its presence was certain,
but when its presence was doubtful, they did not decree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After identifying the תורה-level limit, the גמרא explains the later restriction and why it does not cover a doubtful case.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The חכמים restricted sacred speech when מי רגלים are certainly present on the ground, but did not extend that restriction to doubtful presence.

steps.title: Definite urine restricts speech while it is still wet
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how long definite מי רגלים matter, and שְׁמוּאֵל gives a test: they must still be wet enough to moisten something that touches them.
steps.simpleTranslation: For definite urine, until when? רַב יְהוּדָה says in the name of שְׁמוּאֵל: As long as it can moisten.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks for the limit of the restriction on definite מי רגלים. שְׁמוּאֵל answers with a test of wetness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous ruling established that definite מי רגלים are restricted even after they land. This answer says that, according to שְׁמוּאֵל, the restriction lasts while they can still moisten what touches them.

keyTerms.meaning: the sage whose ruling is reported

phrases.english: And with definite urine, until when?
Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
As long as it can moisten.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 28 limited the restriction to definite מי רגלים; this step asks how long that restriction lasts.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: At what point do definite מי רגלים stop restricting sacred speech?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: According to שְׁמוּאֵל, the restriction lasts while they can still moisten what touches them.

steps.title: Two more reports give the same wetness test
steps.stepSummary: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן and עוּלָּא are also reported as using the moistening test.
steps.simpleTranslation: רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה reports that רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן also said: As long as it can moisten. עוּלָּא said the same.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds two matching statements. Both support the wetness test just given.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These reports do not introduce a new cutoff. They show that the test attributed to שְׁמוּאֵל is also stated by other sages.

keyTerms.meaning: the sage reporting רבי יוחנן’s statement
a sage who gives the same test
another sage who gives the same test

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה
phrases.english: And so too, Rabba bar bar Hana said

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁמַּטְפִּיחִין.
phrases.english: that Rabbi Yohanan said: As long as it can moisten.

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן אָמַר עוּלָּא: כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁמַּטְפִּיחִין.
phrases.english: And so too, Ulla said: As long as it can moisten.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds matching reports for the test stated in step 29.
steps.raayaObject: The moistening test for definite מי רגלים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Reports from רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן and עוּלָּא.

steps.title: A different report uses a visible mark as the cutoff
steps.stepSummary: גְּנִיבָא reports in the name of רַב that the restriction lasts as long as the urine’s mark remains visible.
steps.simpleTranslation: גניבא said in רב’s name: As long as its mark is visible.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא introduces a different test for definite מי רגלים. This report makes a visible mark, rather than the ability to moisten, the cutoff.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A mark might remain after the urine can no longer moisten anything. If so, this report would keep the restriction in place longer than the earlier test.

phrases.english: Geniva said in Rav’s name:
As long as its mark is visible.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a potentially longer-lasting cutoff than the moistening test.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to גְּנִיבָא’s report in the name of רַב, definite מי רגלים remain restricted while their mark is visible.

steps.title: A lenient ruling about feces challenges the visible-mark test
steps.stepSummary: רַב יוֹסֵף challenges גְּנִיבָא’s report: another ruling attributed to רַב permits speech near צוֹאָה once its surface has crusted over.
steps.simpleTranslation: רַב יוֹסֵף says: May his Master forgive גניבא! Even concerning feces, רַב is reported to permit it once the surface forms a crust. Would urine need a stricter rule?
steps.whatsHappening: רַב יוֹסֵף objects to the visible-mark test. He compares it with a seemingly more lenient ruling about צוֹאָה attributed to the same sage, רַב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ruling רַב יוֹסֵף cites, a crusted surface is enough to permit sacred speech near צוֹאָה. He argues that it would be surprising for רַב to require waiting longer for מי רַגְלַיִם.

keyTerms.meaning: is it even necessary to ask?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: שְׁרָא לֵיהּ מָרֵיהּ לִגְנִיבָא,
phrases.english: Rav Yosef said: May his Master forgive Geniva,

phrases.aramaic: הַשְׁתָּא צוֹאָה אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
phrases.english: for even regarding feces, Rav Yehuda said that Rav said
once its surface forms a crust, it is permitted;
is it even necessary to ask about urine?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: שְׁרָא לֵיהּ מָרֵיהּ לִגְנִיבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether the visible-mark test can be attributed to רַב.
steps.kashyaTarget: גְּנִיבָא’s report that רַב restricts מי רַגְלַיִם while their mark remains visible.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רַב יוֹסֵף cites a ruling attributed to רַב that permits sacred speech near crusted צוֹאָה, then questions why מי רַגְלַיִם would remain restricted longer.

steps.title: A second report about feces weakens the objection
steps.stepSummary: אַבָּיֵי points to a different ruling attributed to רַב: צוֹאָה can remain prohibited even when it is like earthenware.
steps.simpleTranslation: אַבָּיֵי says to him: Why rely on that report? Rely instead on this report of רַב: Feces are prohibited even when they are like earthenware.
steps.whatsHappening: אַבָּיֵי pushes back against רַב יוֹסֵף’s proof. He brings a stricter report about צוֹאָה attributed to רַב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רַב יוֹסֵף’s comparison depends on his chosen report about dried צוֹאָה. אַבָּיֵי shows that another report of רַב treats even very dry-looking צוֹאָה as prohibited, so the comparison is not decisive.

keyTerms.meaning: the sage responding to רַב יוֹסֵף
the sage reporting the stricter ruling

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: מַאי חָזֵית דְּסָמְכַתְּ אַהָא,
phrases.english: Abaye said to him: Why did you choose to rely on that report?

phrases.aramaic: סְמוֹךְ אַהָא, דְּאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rely on this one instead: Rabba bar Rav Huna said that Rav said:
Feces, even when like earthenware, are prohibited.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: מַאי חָזֵית דְּסָמְכַתְּ אַהָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Undercuts the report about צוֹאָה that רַב יוֹסֵף used as his proof.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The strength of רַב יוֹסֵף’s objection, not a final ruling about the cutoff for מי רַגְלַיִם.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: His argument relies on one report of רַב while another report attributed to רַב gives a stricter rule for dried צוֹאָה.

steps.title: Two descriptions explain the earthenware comparison
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what כְּחֶרֶס means here, then gives two versions: the צוֹאָה does not crumble when thrown, or it does not crumble when rolled.
steps.simpleTranslation: What counts as feces like earthenware? רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן says: It does not crumble when thrown. Some give the test as: It does not crumble when rolled.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the phrase כְּחֶרֶס means in practice. It then presents two versions of the test for that description.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both versions focus on whether the צוֹאָה crumbles, but they describe different actions: throwing or rolling. This explains the term used in אַבָּיֵי’s response; it does not settle the competing reports about רַב.

phrases.english: And what counts as feces like earthenware?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Hana said that Rabbi Yohanan said:
As long as one throws it and it does not crumble.
And some say: As long as
one rolls it and it does not crumble.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the condition of צוֹאָה named in אַבָּיֵי’s response.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What physical condition is meant by צוֹאָה כְּחֶרֶס?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: One version says it does not crumble when thrown; another says it does not crumble when rolled.
steps.whatToRemember: This passage begins with competing cutoffs for definite מי רַגְלַיִם and ends by clarifying כְּחֶרֶס in the debate about צוֹאָה. It does not yet give a final resolution of those competing reports.

steps.title: Check whether the surface has crusted
steps.stepSummary: רבינא reports how רב יהודה מדיפתי told him to check צואה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: I was standing before רב יהודה מדיפתי. He saw צואה and told me to check whether its surface had crusted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a real-life example of the surface test discussed earlier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The instruction is to look at the surface, not merely to estimate how long the צואה has been there.

keyTerms.meaning: the sage who gives the instruction

phrases.english: Ravina said: I was standing
before Rav Yehuda of Difti
He saw feces and said to me:

phrases.aramaic: עַיֵּין אִי קָרְמוּ פָּנֶיהָ אִי לָא.
phrases.english: Check whether its surface has crusted or not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the earlier discussion of how to assess dried צואה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב יהודה מדיפתי instructs רבינא to check whether the surface of the צואה has crusted.

steps.title: Another version uses cracking as the test
steps.stepSummary: A second version reports a different instruction: check whether the צואה has cracked.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say that he told him: Check whether it is cracked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another version of the same instruction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This version looks for cracks rather than a crusted surface. The גמרא records both versions without choosing between them.

phrases.english: Some say that he said to him this way:
Check whether it is cracked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers another version of the test reported in step 35.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The alternate report instructs רבינא to check whether the צואה has cracked.

steps.title: What is the ruling?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the outcome of the discussion about dried צואה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What was decided about it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from the reported tests to asking for the ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Knowing what was checked does not yet tell us which condition permits recitation. The question asks for the bottom line.

phrases.english: What was decided about it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a ruling after the different descriptions of dried צואה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether צואה described as dry like earthenware still prohibits reciting sacred words nearby.

steps.title: Two sages disagree about dried feces
steps.stepSummary: אמימר prohibits recitation near צואה like earthenware; מר זוטרא permits it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: For feces like earthenware, אמימר says it is prohibited, and מר זוטרא says it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by reporting a disagreement, not yet a final ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions address צואה that has reached the described dry state. They disagree about whether that state is enough to permit recitation nearby.

phrases.english: It was stated: Feces like earthenware—
Ameimar said it is prohibited,
and Mar Zutra said it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the request for a ruling by presenting the two positions.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: אמימר prohibits recitation near צואה like earthenware, while מר זוטרא permits it.

steps.title: רבא states the ruling for feces and urine
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that צואה like earthenware remains prohibited, while מי רגלים are prohibited as long as they moisten.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The ruling is that feces like earthenware are prohibited, and urine is prohibited as long as it moistens.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a ruling for both צואה and מי רגלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For צואה like earthenware, he follows the prohibiting position. For מי רגלים, he states a moisture test; the גמרא will now challenge what that test implies.

keyTerms.meaning: moist enough to dampen what touches it

phrases.english: Rava said: The ruling is:
feces like earthenware are prohibited,
and urine, as long as it moistens.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the disagreement about צואה and adds a ruling about מי רגלים.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: צואה like earthenware remains prohibited; מי רגלים are prohibited while they moisten.

steps.title: A teaching about absorbed or dried urine is introduced
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a teaching that prohibits moist מי רגלים but permits them once absorbed or dried.
steps.simpleTranslation: An objection was raised: Urine is prohibited as long as it moistens; if it was absorbed or dried, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא introduces a teaching to challenge רבא’s moisture test. The challenge itself will come from how the teaching is read in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first, the teaching’s opening agrees with רבא. Its separate mention of absorption and drying gives the questioner room to argue that something besides moisture matters.

phrases.english: An objection was raised: Urine,
as long as it moistens, is prohibited;
if it was absorbed or dried, it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces a source to test רבא’s ruling about מי רגלים.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא’s ruling that the prohibition of מי רגלים lasts as long as they moisten.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The quoted teaching may imply that a visible mark still matters after moisture is gone.

steps.title: Does a visible mark keep urine prohibited?
steps.stepSummary: The questioner reads the teaching to imply that a visible mark of מי רגלים remains prohibited even without moisture.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn’t ‘absorbed’ like ‘dried’? Just as dried urine is permitted when its mark is not visible, so too absorbed urine is permitted when its mark is not visible. But if its mark is visible, it is prohibited even though it no longer moistens!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now spells out the proposed challenge to רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The questioner links ‘absorbed’ to ‘dried’ and makes an invisible mark the condition for permission. If that reading is right, רבא’s moisture test leaves out a case that remains prohibited.

phrases.english: Is it not that ‘absorbed’ is like ‘dried’—
just as ‘dried’ means their mark is not visible,
so too ‘absorbed’ means their mark is not visible?
But if their mark is visible, it is prohibited,
even though they do not moisten!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the proposed inference from the teaching just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא’s moisture-based ruling for מי רגלים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If permission requires the mark to disappear, a visible mark remains prohibited even without moisture.

steps.title: The opening clause supports the opposite inference
steps.stepSummary: The response points out that the same teaching’s opening could imply permission once מי רגלים no longer moisten, even if their mark remains.
steps.simpleTranslation: By your reasoning, consider the first clause: It is prohibited as long as it moistens. That would imply that when its mark is visible, it is permitted!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back by reading the beginning of the same teaching in the opposite direction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The opening says ‘as long as it moistens.’ Read narrowly, that suggests permission when moisture stops, even with a visible mark. That clashes with the questioner’s inference from the later clause.

phrases.english: And by your reasoning, say the first clause:
only as long as it moistens is it prohibited;
but if its mark is visible, it is permitted!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Counters the inference drawn from the teaching’s later clause.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proposed proof that a visible mark remains prohibited without moisture.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The teaching’s opening clause can be used to infer the opposite, so the proposed inference is not secure.

steps.title: The teaching cannot settle the visible-mark question
steps.stepSummary: Because the two inferences conflict, the גמרא draws no further ruling from this teaching.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, nothing can be learned from this teaching on that point.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends this challenge by setting aside both opposing inferences.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The teaching explicitly addresses moist, absorbed, and dried מי רגלים. It does not clearly settle the particular case of a visible mark that no longer moistens, so it does not overturn רבא’s ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: no conclusion can be drawn from it

steps.whatToRemember: Do not infer a ruling about a visible but non-moist mark from this teaching; its clauses point in opposite directions.

phrases.english: Rather, nothing can be inferred from this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: States the result of the conflicting inferences.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: This teaching supplies no decisive proof about מי רגלים whose mark remains visible after they stop moistening.

steps.title: Could the earlier question depend on a disagreement?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא introduces a teaching about spilled מי רגלים and asks whether its two opinions address the earlier question.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us suggest that this depends on תנאים: It is forbidden to recite קריאת שמע opposite a vessel from which מי רגלים were poured. As for spilled מי רגלים themselves, if they were absorbed, it is permitted; if not, it is forbidden. רבי יוסי says: As long as they moisten.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a teaching with two opinions. It is setting up a possible disagreement about when spilled מי רגלים stop being a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion uses whether the liquid was absorbed as its test. רבי יוסי uses whether it still moistens. The גמרא has not yet shown that these are different tests in practice.

keyTerms.meaning: the named sage giving the second opinion

phrases.english: Let us say it depends on a disagreement between tannaim:
A vessel from which urine was poured,
one may not recite Shema opposite it.
And the urine itself that was spilled,
if absorbed, it is permitted; if not absorbed, it is forbidden.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁמַּטְפִּיחִין.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says: As long as they moisten.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the earlier ברייתא yielded no proof, the גמרא suggests that the אמוראים's dispute over moisture vs. a visible mark (steps 29–31) mirrors a dispute between תנאים.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Do the two opinions in this teaching disagree about the visible mark of מי רגלים?

steps.title: What does “absorbed” mean here?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how to understand the first opinion’s terms before comparing it with רבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: What do “absorbed” and “not absorbed” mean when the first teacher says them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to define the first opinion’s words. This prepares the comparison with רבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Absorption might mean that the spot no longer moistens, or that its mark is no longer visible. Those meanings could produce different rulings for a dry but visible spot.

keyTerms.meaning: the first teacher in the quoted teaching

phrases.english: What are “absorbed” and “not absorbed”
that the first teacher says?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The proposed disagreement cannot be tested until the first opinion’s wording is defined.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the first opinion measure absorption by remaining moisture or by a remaining visible mark?

steps.title: The moisture reading leaves no disagreement
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries reading “absorbed” as “no longer moistens” and objects that רבי יוסי would then say the same thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: If “absorbed” means no longer moistening, and “not absorbed” means still moistening, then רבי יוסי says it is forbidden only while it moistens; if its mark remains visible but it does not moisten, it is permitted. That is exactly the first teacher’s view!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests one meaning of “absorbed” and finds a problem. On that reading, the two opinions do not actually disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both opinions use moisture as the cutoff, both permit a dry spot even when its mark remains. That cannot explain why the teaching presents רבי יוסי separately.

phrases.english: If you say “absorbed” means they do not moisten,
and “not absorbed” means they do moisten—
and Rabbi Yosei comes to say:
it is forbidden only as long as they moisten,
but if their mark is visible without moisture, it is permitted,
that is the same as the first teacher!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It tests the moisture-based definition raised in the preceding question.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that defines the first opinion’s absorption test by moisture alone.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That reading makes the first opinion identical to רבי יוסי, leaving no disagreement to explain.

steps.title: A visible mark may be their point of disagreement
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers a different reading: the first opinion tests visibility, while רבי יוסי tests moisture.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, “absorbed” means its mark is not visible, and “not absorbed” means its mark is visible. רבי יוסי then says it is forbidden only while it moistens; if its mark is visible without moisture, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rereads the first opinion so that the two opinions differ. A dry but visible mark becomes the test case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On this reading, the first opinion forbids the visible mark because it counts as “not absorbed.” רבי יוסי permits it once it no longer moistens. This would make the teaching relevant to the earlier question, but the reading is not yet established.

phrases.english: Rather, “absorbed” means their mark is not visible,
and “not absorbed” means their mark is visible.
And Rabbi Yosei comes to say
it is forbidden only as long as they moisten,
but if their mark is visible without moisture, it is permitted.

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: תירוץ — it directly answers why the two opinions might differ; here it also supports the proposed disagreement.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It replaces the reading that made the two opinions identical with one that makes them disagree.
steps.raayaObject: The possibility that תנאים disagree about a visible but dry mark of מי רגלים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The differing wording of the first teacher and רבי יוסי in the quoted teaching.

steps.title: The proposed disagreement is rejected
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the claim that the two opinions must disagree about a dry, visible mark.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone agrees that it is forbidden only as long as the urine moistens; if its mark is visible without moisture, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says the proposed disagreement is not necessary. It begins an alternative reading in which both opinions permit a dry, visible mark.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This removes the visible mark as the proven point of disagreement. The text here does not yet explain what the two opinions disagree about instead; that explanation comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: that is when it is forbidden

phrases.english: No. According to everyone,
it is forbidden only as long as they moisten;
but if their mark is visible without moisture, it is permitted,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It rejects the inference that the teaching establishes a disagreement about a dry, visible mark.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proposed point of disagreement is rejected; the גמרא has not yet completed its alternative explanation of the teaching.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The wording does not force the first opinion to forbid a visible mark after it stops moistening.
